Opening: Lexora is a browser-based workbench for compiler-design assignments. It runs real Flex and Bison specifications and provides a separate educational analysis of program input. Suggested presentation duration: 12–15 minutes. Implementation sources: README.md; frontend/src/App.jsx; backend/services/compiler.js; backend/services/inputAnalysis.js.
Students need to connect compiler theory
with a program they can actually run.
Separate files, terminal commands, and generated C files make early experiments harder to follow.
Program output alone does not explain tokens, syntax structure, scopes, or intermediate code.
Project need: one workspace for execution, diagnostics, and compiler-phase explanations.
Frame these as the project motivation, not findings from a user study. Traditional tool workflows require several commands and do not automatically supply the educational views implemented in Lexora.
Compile selected .l and .y files and execute them with user input.
Expose tokens, AST, symbol table, TAC, optimization, and basic blocks.
Keep browser drafts and provide examples, uploads, and downloads.
Return stage-specific errors, native output, and analysis status.

Explain each objective using a demonstrable feature. Educational analysis is restricted to the built-in C subset. No measured learning improvement is claimed. Implementation sources: README.md; frontend/src/App.jsx; backend/services/compiler.js; backend/services/inputAnalysis.js.

Development: browser :3000, API :3001. Windows execution uses WSL Ubuntu.

Local development topology. Vite serves port 3000 and proxies /api to Express on port 3001. The compiler runs in WSL Ubuntu on Windows or native Bash on Linux. The JavaScript educational analyzer runs in the Node backend. Browser localStorage is local to that browser origin. Sources: frontend/vite.config.js; frontend/src/App.jsx; backend/server.js; backend/services/wslRunner.js; backend/services/compiler.js.
Results: native console + educational analysis tabs
Invalid requests stop at validation. Build failures return the failing phase and available analysis.

Each compilation has two conceptual result paths. In the implementation analyzeInput runs before the native toolchain steps. They are separate computations, not concurrent processes. Invalid requests stop in validation before compiler orchestration. Temporary-directory cleanup runs in finally before the route returns JSON. Sources: frontend/src/App.jsx; backend/routes/compile.js; backend/middleware/validator.js; backend/services/compiler.js.
No application database. Browser drafts and downloaded files are the persistent copies.

Sources: frontend/src/App.jsx (lexora.workspace.v2, lexora.theme, result state); backend/services/tempDir.js (os.tmpdir and lexora-UUID); backend/services/compiler.js; frontend/src/services/files.js. Browser storage survives reloads when available, but clearing site data removes it. It is not cloud sync. Temporary cleanup is attempted in finally; failures are logged. No application database is configured.
A fresh directory for each request
On Windows, WSL accesses the same folder through /mnt/c/...
After the result is assembled, the backend attempts to delete the whole job folder.

Windows example path is schematic, based on os.tmpdir(). The same Windows directory is exposed to Linux through /mnt/c. On Linux the path remains a native path. Source .l and .y line endings normalize to LF. input.txt preserves user input exactly. Cleanup is attempted on success and failure. Sources: backend/services/tempDir.js; backend/services/wslRunner.js; backend/services/compiler.js.

Lex-only skips Bison. Yacc-only must provide its own yylex() and main().

Actual combined-mode order: flex lex.l; bison -d parser.y; normalize references such as y.tab.h to parser.tab.h and regenerate Flex; gcc -o compiler lex.yy.c parser.tab.c -lfl -lm; ./compiler < input.txt. Bison defaults to LALR(1), while supporting other parser table types when requested. Sources: backend/services/compiler.js; https://westes.github.io/flex/manual/Introduction.html; https://www.gnu.org/s/bison/manual/bison.html; https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Overall-Options.html
The displayed educational TAC does not become the native executable.

This distinction prevents a misleading claim that arbitrary user grammars automatically produce all educational outputs. analyzeInput reads inputCode with Lexora’s own tokenizer and recursive-descent parser. The educational TAC never feeds GCC. Native diagnostics remain authoritative for the user-supplied program. Sources: README.md; backend/services/inputAnalysis.js; backend/services/compiler.js.
The optimizer transforms TAC. Basic-block detection partitions the original TAC.

The implementation computes tokens and then parseAST(input), whose parser handles its own tokenization. This diagram shows the conceptual learning phases. Semantic analysis and TAC both use the AST. Basic blocks use original TAC. Sources: backend/services/inputAnalysis.js; tokenExtractor.js; astGenerator.js; semanticAnalyzer.js; tacGenerator.js; optimizer.js; basicBlocks.js.
Multiplication groups 3 and 4 before the addition to 2.
x is an integer variable declared in global scope.

Observed directly using analyzeInput("int x = 2 + 3 * 4;"). Nine tokens. AST root is Declaration, datatype int, variable x. Expression has addition at root and multiplication in the right branch. Symbol x has type int, kind variable, global scope, declared true and used false. This is educational analysis, not a claim that the calculator grammar accepts C declarations. Source: backend/services/inputAnalysis.js.
Constant folding evaluates arithmetic. Constant propagation substitutes known values.
This example has one basic block because it contains no branches.

Actual output of analyzeInput("int x = 2 + 3 * 4;"). Original TAC: t1 = 3 * 4; t2 = 2 + t1; x = t2. Optimized TAC: t1 = 12; t2 = 14; x = 14. The optimizer retains three assignments in this example, so do not claim instruction-count reduction or measured speedup. Source: backend/services/optimizer.js and observed analyzer output.

Versions derive from package.json dependency ranges, not installed-version measurements. Frontend uses React 19 and Vite 8, superseding older architecture notes mentioning React 18. Avoid claiming exact toolchain versions unless measured on the demonstration machine. Sources: frontend/package.json; backend/package.json; backend/services/wslRunner.js; Dockerfile.
Load Calculator, choose Lex + Yacc, then Compile.
Show the console, syntax tree, and TAC tabs.
Keep a newline after the expression. The bundled grammar uses EOL to finish a result.

Verified using backend/services/compiler.js with the bundled examples/calculator/calculator.l and calculator.y and exact stdin "3 + 5 * 2\n". Observed success true, stdout "13\n", no errors. Saved observation in private build files. The grammar requires EOL after each expression, so keep the trailing newline. This is an actual backend result, not a UI screenshot.

It includes some native lexer integration checks. Also verified calculator compilation separately. Repository regression tests cover additional modes, timeouts and request errors but were not rerun for this deck. Sources: test output; backend/services/wslRunner.js; backend/middleware/validator.js.
Educational C subset, selected .l/.y targets, and local browser drafts.
Add arrays, structs, pointers, and more complete C semantics.
No extra C/header project files, cloud workspace sync, or full C frontend.
Add isolated execution workers before accepting untrusted public submissions.
Uploaded C actions run with the backend user’s privileges. This is a trusted-use workbench.

These limits describe actual implementation boundaries. This is a trusted local workbench. Native C actions execute with backend-user privileges. WSL, timeouts and per-job folders are not a security sandbox. Public untrusted submissions require real isolation. Sources: README.md; backend/services/wslRunner.js. Future work is proposed, not implemented.
Browser drafts and temporary build files
A separate analyzer for compiler concepts

Close by linking the project back to its objective: a student can submit real specifications, see native results, and examine compiler concepts in the same interface. Emphasize integration as the contribution. Invite questions about the separate analysis pipeline, storage or generated files.
